newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Ex-cop says terror part of old SAfrica arsenal.
newsitem.headline: Ex-cop says terror part of old SAfrica arsenal.

text.p: An apartheid-era policeman jailed for a 1988 massacre of 11 people told South Africa's "truth commission" on Wednesday that the old white government used terror to fight black liberation groups.

"Terrorism worked to break the rules, but when the authorities broke the rules (they) turned the terror back on the terrorists," said Brian Mitchell, who was sentenced to death in 1992 for killing 11 blacks in a massacre in KwaZulu-Natal province.
His sentence was later commuted to 30 years in jail and is now testifying before the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, which he hopes will grant him amnesty for his crime.

Mitchell, 39, said top secret documents drafted by police chiefs had detailed measures their footsoldiers could take to cut off support for Nelson Mandela's then-banned African National Congress (ANC).
The movement took up arms against the white minority government, which considered it to be a "terrorist" group.
The government's strategy led to active police support for the ANC's rivals in the mainly Zulu-based Inkatha Freedom Party.
Helping Inkatha was intended to stem ANC encroachment in KwaZulu-Natal province, he said.
The programme of support led to the killing of 11 people aged from four to 66 at a funeral vigil near Pietermaritzburg eight years ago, for which he was convicted.
The victims were shot dead at close range by four shotgun-wielding policemen under orders from Mitchell, who said he had mistakenly thought the home was occupied by ANC supporters.
"It was a terrible mistake. The next morning I saw so many innocent people had been killed and what a disaster it was," Mitchell said.

His testimony bore out evidence presented during the murder trial of former defence minister Magnus Malan that the state fuelled violence by a divide and rule policy of supporting one side in the violence in KwaZulu-Natal.
Malan and 19 others were acquitted last Friday of murder charges from the 1987 killing of 13 people near the port city of Durban.
But the judge found that the attack was almost certainly carried out by Inkatha members trained by the defence force.
Mitchell is the first apartheid-era policeman to appear before the amnesty committee of the truth commission chaired by Nobel peace laureate Archbishop Desmond Tutu.

The body can grant amnesty to perpetrators of human rights abuses from across the political spectrum if it believes they have made full and honest confessions and that the crimes were politically motivated.
